questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Get on like a house on fire

Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Get on like a house on fire

options.text: Get on extremely well with someone
options.html: Get on extremely well with someone

options.text: Feel a lot of affection for one particular person, often without knowing why
options.html: Feel a lot of affection for one particular person, often without knowing why

options.text: Do something good for someone you have done something bad to in the past
options.html: Do something good for someone you have done something bad to in the past

questions.solution:
The solution is Get on extremely well with someone,

Key Points

  • The most appropriate meaning of the given idiom 'Get on like a house on fire' is Get on extremely well with someone.(किसी के साथ बहुत अच्छे से घुलना-मिलना)
  • Therefore option 2 is the correct option.

Additional Information

  • Let's discuss about idioms:

    • For example:- 
      • Get your act together - Get organized and do things effectively.(संगठित हो जाओ और काम प्रभावी ढंग से करो)
      • Back against the wall - Stuck in a difficult circumstance with no escape.(ऐसी कठिन परिस्थिति में फँस गया हूँ जहाँ से निकलने का कोई रास्ता नहीं है)

questions.question: Select the correct idiom that can substitute the italicised group of words in the given sentence. He really stinks and smells foul after a hard session at the gym.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the correct idiom that can substitute the italicised group of words in the given sentence.

He really stinks and smells foul after a hard session at the gym.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is pen and ink.
 
Key Points
  • The given phrase "stinks and smells foul" refers to a very unpleasant smell (बहुत बुरी तरह से बदबू आना).
    • Example: After jogging in the park during summer, he stinks and smells foul.
  • The correct idiomatic expression "pen and ink" is used to imply something that smells bad (बदबू).
    • Example: When he removed his shoes, the whole room was filled with pen and ink.
  • Hence, the correct idiom is pen and ink.
Therefore, the correct answer is "Option 3".
 
Additional Information
  • An old flame: Refers to a former lover or someone with whom one had a romantic relationship (पुराना प्यार).
    • Example: During the high school reunion, he was surprised to see his old flame.
  • An iron will: Means having a very strong determination or willpower (मजबूत इच्छाशक्ति).
    • Example: Despite the challenges, she completed her degree with an iron will.
  • Lame excuse: A weak or poor excuse for something, not convincing (कमजोर बहाना).
    • Example: He gave a lame excuse for his absence, saying his alarm clock didn't ring.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Steer clear of
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Steer clear of

options.text: Loose temper and react furiously to someone
options.html: Loose temper and react furiously to someone

options.text: Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you
options.html: Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you

options.text: Show someone how to do a job or activity
options.html: Show someone how to do a job or activity

options.text: Be kind and empathetic to someone
options.html: Be kind and empathetic to someone

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: "Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you."

Key Points

  • The idiom "steer clear of" means to avoid or stay away from something, often due to danger, trouble, or undesirable consequences.
  • It implies an effort to keep a safe and cautious distance from a particular situation or person.
    • Example: After hearing about the recent issues at the company, Reena decided to steer clear of any involvement in office politics.
  • From the above example, it is clear that "avoid some or something because it is dangerous for you" is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
  • Hence, the correct answer is "Avoid someone or something because it is dangerous for you".

Therefore, the correct answer is "Option 2".

Additional Information

  • Some idioms that convey a similar meaning to "Steer clear of":
    • Keep one's distance: Stay away or avoid getting too close.
      • Example: It's wise to keep one's distance from any wild animal.
    • Keep at arm's length: To maintain a safe or cautious distance.
      • Example: Since going to college, he has kept his old friends at arm's length.
    • Stay out of harm's way: To avoid situations that could be dangerous or harmful.
      • Example: He asked the children to stay out of his arm's way while he made dinner.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Step up to the plate
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Step up to the plate
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option (4) i.e. 'Take control of a situation'.

Key Points

  • To "step up to the plate": To take responsibility or take action in a challenging situation (कठिन परिस्थिति में जिम्मेदारी लेना या कार्रवाई करना)
    • Example: When the team leader fell ill, Anita stepped up to the plate and ensured the project was completed on time.
  • Take control of a situation: (किसी स्थिति का नियंत्रण लेना)
  • This option 4 directly reflects the idiom's meaning related to taking responsibility and action, especially when it is needed or when facing challenges.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'Take control of a situation'.

Additional Information

  • Think about a crisis: This does not capture the proactive, responsibility-taking nature of the idiom.
  • Plan for better performance: This focuses on preparation, not the comprehensive action or taking charge implied by the idiom.
  • Implement a plan: While part of taking control, the idiom more broadly signifies seizing initiative or responsibility, which goes beyond mere implementation.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom that can be substituted in the following sentence. The new routine will suit you to a T .
questions.questionHtml:

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'exactly'.

Key Points

  • The most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom "to a T" in the given sentence is: exactly.
  • Explanation: The idiom "to a T" means perfectly or exactly suited to someone's needs or preferences. (किसी की आवश्यकताओं या प्राथमिकताओं के लिए बिल्कुल उपयुक्त)
  • In the context of the sentence, it suggests that the new routine will be a perfect fit for the person, addressing their requirements or desires precisely.
  • Options 1 (nicely) and 2 (a little bit) do not capture the sense of precise suitability conveyed by the idiom. Option 4 (very poorly) is the opposite, indicating a poor fit.
  • Therefore, option 3, "exactly," is the most appropriate meaning in this context.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Till the cows come home

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2, 'For a long, long time'.

Thus and so, option 2 is the correct meaning to the idiomatic phrase.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Touch and go
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Touch and go
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2) i.e.'Uncertain'.

  • 'Touch and go' means 'uncertain',temporary', 'ever-changing'.
  • Related: 'Vague','Bizarre','Strange','hanging by thread'.
  • Contexts: 'The newly passed political law', 'The weather conditions','The result of an exam','The situations of life'.
  • Sentence instance:
    • ​The newly passed political law is always touch and go till the time it is implemented. 
    •  The result of an exam is always touch and go till the time it is out. 
    • The weather conditions in Bombay are always touch and go (uncertain).
  • Antonyms: 'Unchanging', 'Undoubted', 'Peaceful', 'At ease', 'Sure', 'Certain'.
  • Form of the word and origin: 'Idiom', '16th century, England'.

​Thus and so, option 2.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Make a beeline for
questions.questionHtml:

Make a beeline for
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 4) i.e. 'Go straight to'.

  • 'Make a beeline for' is used 'figuratively, metaphorically or related to' in context. 
  • Let's consider it in this way: 'the movement of bee/bees is always in queue/straight line, following one after the other'. The bee/bees do not deviate from its/their path. The way a bee/bees moves in a straight line, is the same way the meaning of 'Make a beeline for' is considered. 
  • 'Make a beeline for' is 'to go straight without getting distracted', 'to aim for', 'to follow something blindly'. (like bees following one another in a straight line to aim for something) 
  • Contexts: 'Congregation (religious flock, following a religion which others are following)', 'aim for a better result in the exam', 'to go from one room to another for a purpose (to fetch a book, called by someone, etc).
  • In a sentence: People who migrate to the United States of America make a beeline for Christianity. This is known as 'Congregation'.
  •                          When the manager called the employee to his cabin, the employee made a beeline to the manager's cabin. 

Thus and so, option 4)

questions.question: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Tide over
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Tide over
questions.solution:
The correct answer is- to overcome​.

Key Points

  • Let's look at the meaning of the given idiom:
    • Tide over- to support or enable to survive temporarily
  • Example: 
    • I need money to tide us over until payday.
       

​ ​​​​Additional Information  

  • Let's look at the origin of the idiom:
    • The original 'tiding over' was a seafaring term and derives ultimately from 'tide' being synonymous with 'time'.
    • The literal meaning was 'in the absence of wind to fill the sails, float with the tide'.
    • This usage was recorded by the English seaman Captain John Smith.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. Egg on
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Egg on
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'encourage'.

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: Egg on means to encourage, urge or dare someone to continue doing something, usually something unwise.
    • For example, Nobody egged him on into doing that.
  • From the given options, the first option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "Egg on" that it is all about to place an egg somewhere, but the correct answer is option 1. So be careful while dealing with such questions.
     

Additional Information

  • The idiom/phrase originates from: This phrase usually carries a negative connotation. The verb egged, from which the phrase to "egg on" is derived, has been in the English language since approximately 1200. It is derived from the Old Norse word eggja, which means to incite or provoke. The idiom to "egg on" first appeared in the mid-1500s.

questions.question: Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom. High time
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

High time
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'past the appropriate time'.

Key Points

  • Given Idiom: High time means a long-awaited occasion or past the appropriate time.
    • For example, It's high time this leakage of information was put a stop to.
  • From the given options, the first option is the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
     

Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

Mistake Points

  • We may think from the phrase "High time" that it is all about the time to celebrate something, but the correct answer is option 1. So be careful while dealing with such questions.
     

Additional Information

  • The idiom/phrase originates from: This phrase originated in the 13th century and it refers to the warmest time in the day. Since people of that era were mostly farmers, this time marked the turning point in the day when you must have either gotten so much work done on the land or you begin doing so immediately. With time, the phrase got to be used to refer to a time when any activity has to be started given that the best time is passed.

The phrase, in the long run, means in the coming future.

Regularly means in uniform intervals of time.

Eventually means after a long period of time.

Immediately means at once or instantly.

Intermittently means at irregular intervals.

It is clear that the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom is given by the word "eventually".

Hence, option 2 is the correct answer.

questions.solution: The idiom "in the doldrums" means feeling sad, dejected, and lacking energy or enthusiasm. The word "doldrums" refers to a region near the equator where there is little wind and ships often get stuck for days or weeks. Example: At that time, Freddie had just lost his job and was in the doldrums.
